title: Pesticides and Genetic Engineering
subtitle: Fighting disease vectors with chemicals, sterile insects and modified genes
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate procedures that can be employed to prevent the spread of disease, including but not limited to: use of pesticides, genetic engineering

Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse how human-induced pressures can drive the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria and Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane (DDT)-resistant mosquitoes
Conduct a secondary-source investigation to evaluate the use of biotechnologies on the prevalence of mosquito-borne diseases
Evaluate the potential societal benefits of using genetic technologies to manage infectious diseases
inquiryQuestion: How can the spread of infectious diseases be controlled?
lessonIntent: Students can explain how pesticide use drives DDT-resistant mosquitoes by natural selection, evaluate the sterile insect technique and genetic technologies for vector control, and weigh their societal benefits.
examSkill: Compare vector-control strategies on effectiveness, resistance potential, ecological impact and societal benefit.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, pesticides and genetic engineering for disease control. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Pesticides and Genetic Engineering (Year 12 Biology, Module 7, Lesson 17)

scenes.heading: Beating a pest with infertility
scenes.body: From the late 1950s, the USDA released millions of sterile screwworm flies every week. By 1982 the screwworm was gone from the US.
scenes.callout: How do you wipe out a pest by flooding it with infertile males?
scenes.caption: The sterile insect technique eradicated screwworm from the US by 1982.

voiceover.text: OK, here's one of the strangest success stories in pest control. From the late nineteen fifties, a US Department of Agriculture scientist named Edward Knipling led a program releasing sterile flies, on purpose, across the southern United States. We're talking millions of irradiated, infertile male screwworm flies, every single week. Screwworms were a horror for farmers, because their larvae eat the living flesh of cattle. The plan sounds backwards, fighting a pest by adding more of it. But by nineteen eighty two, the screwworm had been eradicated from the whole country. So how do you wipe out a species by flooding it with infertile males? That's where we're headed, along with chemicals and genetic engineering, the modern toolkit for controlling the insects that spread disease.

scenes.heading: Pesticides attack the vector
scenes.body: Many diseases reach us through an insect vector. Pesticides break that link by killing the insect.

bullets.text: They target the insect nervous system, growth or gut, like DDT, pyrethroids and Bt toxin.
Pyrethroid-treated bed nets are a frontline tool against malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
Heavy spraying is a human-induced selection pressure: DDT-resistant mosquitoes evolved.

scenes.secondary: DDT was hugely effective at first, but it bioaccumulates up food chains and selected for resistant mosquitoes, so it is now banned or restricted in most countries.
scenes.callout: Kill the vector, break the chain, but resistance follows.
scenes.caption: Pesticides kill insect vectors; heavy use selects for resistant mosquitoes.

voiceover.text: Let's start with the oldest tool, chemical pesticides. Many serious diseases, like malaria and dengue, reach humans through an insect vector, usually a mosquito. So one obvious strategy is to break that link by killing the insect. Pesticides attack the insect's nervous system, its growth or its gut, which is how DDT, the pyrethroids and the bacterial Bt toxin work. A great example is the pyrethroid treated bed net, a frontline defence against malaria mosquitoes. But here's the catch. Heavy spraying is a human induced selection pressure. A few mosquitoes already carry mutations that let them survive, and spraying kills the rest, so the survivors breed and resistance spreads. That's how DDT resistant mosquitoes emerged, the same logic as antibiotic resistant bacteria. DDT is the cautionary tale, because it also builds up in food chains, and today it's banned or restricted almost everywhere.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Vector control: reducing disease spread by targeting the organism that transmits the pathogen.
Sterile insect technique: releasing sterile males so wild females produce no viable offspring.
Gene drive: a genetic system that pushes a chosen allele through a population faster than normal inheritance.
Non-target effect: an unintended impact on organisms other than the pest being controlled.

scenes.callout: Different tools, same goal: stop the vector spreading the pathogen.
scenes.caption: Vector control, sterile insect technique, gene drive, non-target effect.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the key terms. Vector control is the umbrella idea, reducing disease spread by targeting the organism that carries the pathogen, rather than the pathogen itself. The sterile insect technique means releasing sterile males so that wild females mate but produce no viable offspring. A gene drive is a genetic system that pushes a chosen gene through a population much faster than normal Mendelian inheritance would, so a trait can sweep through in just a few generations. And a non target effect is any unintended impact on organisms other than the pest you're aiming at. Keep those four in mind, because the rest of the lesson is about weighing them against each other.

scenes.heading: The sterile insect technique
scenes.body: SIT turns the pest's own reproduction against it: mate with a sterile male, and you get no offspring.

bullets.text: Mass-rear the insect, sterilise the males, then release them in huge numbers.
Wild females that mate with sterile males produce no offspring, so the population collapses over generations.
It is species-specific, leaves no chemical residue, and resistance is very unlikely to evolve.

scenes.secondary: Why so hard to resist? Resistance would need females that can recognise and avoid sterile males, and mass-reared sterile males look and behave like wild ones.
scenes.callout: Turn the pest's own mating against it.
scenes.caption: SIT collapses a population using sterile males; it is species-specific and very hard to resist.

voiceover.text: So here's how the sterile insect technique works, the screwworm trick from the hook. First you mass rear the insect, millions of them. Then you sterilise the males, usually with radiation. Then you release them in overwhelming numbers, far more than the wild males. When a wild female mates, she's far more likely to pair with a sterile male, and that mating produces no offspring. Repeat that generation after generation, and the population collapses. It has three big advantages. It's species specific, because sterile males only compete for mates within their own species. It leaves no chemical residue. And resistance is very unlikely to evolve, because the only way to resist would be for females to recognise and avoid sterile males, and those males look and behave just like wild ones. There's almost nothing for selection to grab onto.

scenes.heading: Genetic tools for control
scenes.body: Genetic engineering gives newer, more targeted ways to suppress vectors or block transmission.

bullets.text: Self-limiting GM males (OX513A): their offspring die before adulthood, so releases must continue.
Gene drive: spreads a trait through a population fast, powerful but hard to reverse and still experimental.
Bt crops: a plant makes its own bacterial Cry toxin, cutting external pesticide spraying.

scenes.secondary: Watch this one: Wolbachia is NOT genetic modification. It is a natural bacterium that, once in a mosquito, lowers its ability to transmit dengue. No foreign DNA is added.
scenes.callout: Modify the insect, or just lower its ability to spread disease.
scenes.caption: OX513A, gene drive and Bt crops are GM; Wolbachia is a natural bacterium, not GM.

voiceover.text: Now the cutting edge, genetic tools. The first is self limiting GM males, like the strain OX five one three A. They're engineered so that when they mate with wild females, the offspring die before reaching adulthood. That suppresses the population, but because the gene removes itself, you have to keep releasing them. The second is a gene drive, which uses gene editing to force a trait through a population far faster than normal. It's incredibly powerful, but hard to reverse and still largely experimental, which raises real biosafety concerns. The third is Bt crops, where a plant is engineered to make its own bacterial Cry toxin, killing the insects that eat it and cutting spraying. And here's a point examiners love. Wolbachia is not genetic modification. It's a natural bacterium that, once inside a mosquito, lowers its ability to transmit dengue, and no foreign DNA is added.

scenes.heading: Weighing the societal benefits
scenes.body: Genetic technologies for vector control are judged on what they do for people, not just for mosquito numbers.

bullets.text: Health: fewer infections, deaths and hospital admissions from mosquito-borne disease.
Economic: less spending on treatment and spraying, more days at work and school.
Environmental: less insecticide, fewer non-target effects, less resistance.
Concerns: cost, long-term ecological unknowns, and the need for community consent.

scenes.callout: Benefits to people, weighed against risk and consent.
scenes.caption: Societal benefits: health, economic and environmental, weighed against cost, unknowns and consent.

voiceover.text: So how do you evaluate these technologies for society, not just for the mosquitoes? Start with health, because fewer infected mosquitoes means fewer cases, fewer deaths and fewer hospital admissions. Then the economics, less money spent on treatment and spraying, and more people well enough to work and go to school. There's an environmental benefit too, because targeted genetic methods reduce insecticide use, so there are fewer non target effects and less pressure for resistance. Australia has tested this. In Innisfail, in north Queensland, CSIRO and partners released male Aedes aegypti carrying Wolbachia, whose matings with wild females produce no offspring, and the local population fell by more than eighty percent. But a strong evaluation weighs the concerns as well, the cost of rearing millions of insects, the unknown long term ecological effects, especially for gene drives, and the need for communities to agree before anything is released.

scenes.heading: Compare two strategies
scenes.question: A health authority must choose between spraying a chemical pesticide and using the sterile insect technique against a mosquito vector. Compare them on effectiveness, resistance and ecological impact.
scenes.coachNote: Take each criterion in turn and contrast the two approaches.
steps: Effectiveness: pesticide acts fast but broadly; SIT is slower, needing several generations, but highly targeted.
Resistance: pesticide use selects for resistant insects; resistance to SIT is very unlikely, with almost nothing to select for.
Ecological impact: pesticides can bioaccumulate and harm non-target species; SIT is species-specific with no residue.
Trade-off: SIT is cleaner and resistance-proof but expensive and needs sustained releases.
Answer: SIT is more sustainable and targeted; pesticide is faster and cheaper but breeds resistance and harms non-targets ✓
scenes.caption: Pesticide versus SIT compared on effectiveness, resistance and ecology.

voiceover.text: Let's do the kind of comparison the exam asks for. A health authority has to choose between spraying a chemical pesticide and using the sterile insect technique against a mosquito vector. Compare them on three criteria. First, effectiveness. The pesticide acts fast but broadly, hitting lots of insects quickly, whereas SIT is slower, needing several generations to collapse the population, but it's highly targeted. Second, resistance. Pesticide use selects for resistant insects over time, while resistance to SIT is very unlikely, because there's almost no trait for selection to act on. Third, ecological impact. Pesticides can bioaccumulate and harm non target species, while SIT is species specific and leaves no residue. So the trade off is that SIT is cleaner and hard to resist, but expensive and needs sustained releases, while the pesticide is faster and cheaper, but breeds resistance and harms other species.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking pesticide resistance means the pesticide changed or got weaker. The chemical is unchanged; the insect population evolved.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: assuming Wolbachia mosquitoes are genetically modified. They are not, Wolbachia is a natural bacterium and no foreign DNA is inserted. Also remember, self-limiting GM mosquitoes cannot spread their gene through the wild population without continued releases.
scenes.mistakeTag: What resistance means, and what counts as GM
scenes.callout: The insect evolves, not the chemical; Wolbachia is natural, not GM.
scenes.caption: Resistance is an insect population change; Wolbachia is not genetic modification.

voiceover.text: Two traps to watch. Trap one, thinking pesticide resistance means the pesticide itself changed or got weaker. It didn't. The chemical is exactly as toxic as it always was. What changed is the mosquito population, because mutations, in things like the nerve sodium channel or detox enzymes, let some individuals survive, and those survivors bred. The pesticide still kills susceptible insects, it just no longer kills all of them. Trap two, assuming Wolbachia mosquitoes are genetically modified. They're not. Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium, and the mosquito's own genome is unchanged. And remember, self limiting GM mosquitoes like OX five one three A can't establish their gene in the wild on their own, because the offspring die, so the effect only lasts while releases continue.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: After years of spraying the same pesticide, it stops controlling a mosquito population. Explain why, and suggest why switching to the sterile insect technique would not face the same problem.
answerSteps: Rare resistant insects existed by random mutation before spraying began.
The pesticide killed susceptible insects and selected for the resistant ones, which then bred.
Over years the population became dominated by resistant insects, so the chemical stopped working.
Resisting SIT would need females that recognise and avoid sterile males, which look and behave like wild males.
Answer: pesticide resistance evolved by natural selection; SIT gives selection almost nothing to act on ✓
scenes.caption: Pesticide resistance evolves by selection; SIT gives selection almost nothing to act on.

voiceover.text: Quick check. After years of spraying the same pesticide, it stops controlling a mosquito population. Explain why, and suggest why switching to the sterile insect technique wouldn't face the same problem. Pause and reason it through. Right. Rare resistant mosquitoes already existed by random mutation, before spraying began. Each spray killed the susceptible insects and spared the resistant ones, which then bred. Over years, the population became dominated by resistant mosquitoes, so the chemical stopped working. That's natural selection, driven by a human induced pressure. Why would SIT escape this? Because the only way to resist it would be for females to recognise and avoid sterile males, and those males look and behave just like wild ones. With almost nothing for selection to act on, resistance is very unlikely to build.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Vector control breaks the chain of infection by targeting the insect that carries the pathogen.
Heavy pesticide use is a human-induced selection pressure that produced DDT-resistant mosquitoes.
The sterile insect technique collapses a population using sterile males; it is species-specific and hard to resist.
Genetic tools include self-limiting GM males, gene drives and Bt crops; Wolbachia is natural, not GM.
Evaluate genetic technologies on health, economic and environmental benefits, against cost, risk and consent.
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating a control method? Weigh effectiveness, resistance potential, ecological impact and benefit to society.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: vector control, resistance, SIT, genetic tools, and societal benefits.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, vector control breaks the chain of infection by targeting the insect that carries the pathogen. Second, heavy pesticide use is a human induced selection pressure, and that's how DDT resistant mosquitoes emerged. Third, the sterile insect technique collapses a population using sterile males, and it's species specific and very hard to resist. Fourth, the genetic tools to know are self limiting GM males, gene drives and Bt crops, while Wolbachia is a natural bacterium, not genetic modification. And fifth, evaluate genetic technologies on their health, economic and environmental benefits, weighed against cost, risk and community consent. See you next lesson.
